Meanwhile, Ring paced about at home in the most agonizing anxiety. When Alette heard the mistress leave the house, she went back in to him and stood sobbing with her apron before her eyes. He had brought ruin upon her; now the mistress would dismiss her—why had he not let her remain what she had been? Before, she had conducted herself like a decent girl, and now! Oh, dear Jesus, that things should go this way for her—what was to become of her now? There was nothing for it but to go straight off and cast herself away— Ring promised not to abandon her and asked her merely to remain calm and do her work as though nothing had happened. He would see if he could smooth matters over so that nothing more came of it.

Then he walked up and down the sitting room, stopping every now and then and cursing the damned accident that had played him such an intricate trick. He writhed at the thought of all that he would have to go through with Constance. She would not be merciful, he thought, but in the end he consoled himself that it would all blow over after some time had passed. At this point in his reflections, he felt the need to revive himself with a glass of cognac and water. Why was Constance always like that—it was her fault that things went so badly. Why did they not live together like two turtledoves?

Every moment he was at the window peering out; now and then he stood out in the entrance hall and listened.

The longer it went on, the more uneasy he became; his mouth was drawn into a sullen grimace, his eyebrows formed a sharp angle, and his forehead lay in thick, baggy folds. He dreaded terribly the moment when she would enter and was at the same time in torment because she did not come.

At last he heard someone at the front door. He went out and opened it.

Constance passed him calmly and began taking off her outer garments. Then she went into the sitting room, sat down on the sofa, and picked up the evening paper.

Ring sank onto a chair some distance away and remained sitting bent forward, with his elbow on his knee and his hand shading his eyes. Now and then he glanced over at his wife, but lacked the courage to address her.

At last he gathered his courage and said, “Can you forgive me, Constance?”

She put the newspaper aside, looked at him as though about to say something, but gave it up and took up the paper again.

“This day shall be a turning point in my life,” he began.

“Spare me your phrases,” she said dryly. “I cannot bear to listen to them.”

“I know I have offended you cruelly,” he stammered, “and I will accept whatever penance you impose upon me—whatever—”

“What I have to say is not much,” she interrupted him with a motion of her hand. “When you are having relations with my servant girl—”

“I am not having relations with anyone.”

“When you are having relations with my servant girl, then it goes without saying that I wish to be spared your company. If you want her—then by all means, but then you must leave me in peace. I have consented to be your wife—that is bad enough, but I will not be one of your mistresses.” She rose and made to leave the room.

Ring thought she had never been so lovely and so desirable as at that moment. She was an entirely different woman. A terror of losing her shot through his mind like a vicious stab; he sprang up and placed himself in her way.

“Scorn me, trample on me, spit on me, kill me!” he cried. “I am a wretch, a miserable fellow who did not know what a treasure I possessed, a man unworthy to untie your shoelace, but I love you, Constance—no, let me speak—I love and adore you; I lie in the dust and kiss your feet—I care for no one in the world but you, whatever you may believe.” He held his hands to his head and writhed as though in convulsions.

“Nonsense,” she said with a grimace. “You bore me.”

“Yes, I know it—I know it, and that is my eternal torment. You have never loved me, not in the least. And then at times you have behaved in such a way that I almost had to imagine that you cared for me—I have been in a maze, I have. Oh, Constance, if you had loved me, you could have made a different man of me. How I have languished for your love; that is what is to blame.” His voice was lost in weeping. He sank to his knees and hid his face in her dress.

“Get up—you are drunk,” she said unwillingly.

“I am just as sober at this moment as you yourself, Constance.” He looked up at her with the look of a punished dog. “I will not get up; I shall lie here until you say that you have forgiven me.”

Constance felt a fellow human being’s compassion for him; it pained her to see him so humiliated. “But how do you expect me to be able to believe you?” she said.

“No, Constance—it is true, it is all too true—oh, but do it nevertheless, this one time, and you shall have thanks and honor for it; when you have once come to trust me anew, and perhaps feel a kind of affection for me because for many years I have been undemanding and faithful and have never complained, then it will do you good to think that it was you who saved me. Do not thrust me away, for without you I shall perish.” He was still on his knees, holding her dress in both hands and kissing it.

Constance was caught up in this deep emotion. She bowed her head and began to weep.

“There is an old saying that it is better to give than to receive,” he continued in the same passionately pleading voice. “Look at me, Constance, lying here and begging, while you stand there so far above me and hold my fate in your hand; do not be merciless, but let yourself be moved, Constance.”

“It is not out of hardness,” she said in a tearful voice, “but what has happened cannot simply be erased from our lives.”

“Yes, it can, it can, Constance; oh, try, try—receive me back into your favor and put me on trial.”

“Get up and sit down—I want to ask you something.”

He obeyed like a schoolboy. She took a seat directly opposite him.

“Since it appears that you take this as seriously as it is,” she said, while smoothing her handkerchief on her lap and folding it into a small square, “then perhaps I may expect you to answer me truthfully.”

“Yes, you may rely on that, Constance.”

“Then let me know how far things have gone between you and her.”

“Gone? They have not gone anywhere at all. What could they have gone to, apart from what you saw? That is bad enough.”
